name: advice
system: You are an advisor answering a person's question. Base your advice only on the point provided. You may add a brief remark that sets the tone, but no new advice. Never write more than three sentences.

options: Open with a short remark, in your own voice, that shows you understand how the person may be feeling.
Go straight to the advice, with no greeting, sympathy or encouragement.
Give the advice as firm, direct instructions, starting each sentence with a verb.
Describe what works well for most people in plain statements rather than commands, and leave it to the person to decide what to adopt.
Sound calm and even, with no exclamation marks.
Give the reason behind each piece of advice.
State the advice only, with no reasons or explanation.
Write in a relaxed, conversational way, using contractions and everyday phrasing, but no slang.
Write formally, with no contractions or slang.

train.q: I keep forgetting to take my daily medication. What can I do?
facts: Tying the dose to a daily routine, such as brushing your teeth, makes it easier to remember.

train.q: I have an exam next week. How should I study?
facts: Spreading study over several days works better than cramming the night before.

train.q: How do I start saving money?
facts: An automatic transfer to savings on payday makes saving consistent.

train.q: I'm about to sign a lease for an apartment. What should I watch for?
facts: Read the whole lease before signing it.

train.q: I have too many tasks at work. How do I cope?
facts: Listing tasks and ranking them by urgency and importance shows what to do first.

train.q: I have trouble falling asleep. What helps?
facts: Going to bed and waking up at the same times each day helps regulate the body clock.

train.q: I can't stay focused when I study. Any advice?
facts: Keeping your phone out of reach removes the most common distraction.

train.q: How should I pay down my credit card debt?
facts: Paying more than the minimum each month reduces the interest you pay.

train.q: How can I make my team's meetings more useful?
facts: Sending an agenda beforehand lets people come prepared.

train.q: I want to start exercising again after a long break. How?
facts: Starting with short sessions and building up gradually lowers the risk of injury.

heldout.q: My back hurts from sitting at a desk all day. What can I do?
facts: Raising your screen to eye level reduces strain.

heldout.q: How can I remember more of what I read?
facts: Summarizing the material in your own words strengthens memory.

heldout.q: I'm about to make a big purchase. How do I avoid regretting it?
facts: Comparing prices from several sellers helps you find a fair deal.

heldout.q: I lost my wallet. What should I do first?
facts: Cancelling your bank cards right away prevents fraudulent charges.

heldout.q: A client keeps asking for extra work outside our agreement. What do I do?
facts: Putting the agreed scope in writing gives you something to point to.

test.q: How should I prepare for a doctor's appointment?
facts: Writing down your symptoms and questions beforehand helps you cover everything.

test.q: What's a good way to learn a new language?
facts: Short daily practice works better than occasional long sessions.

test.q: How do I make a budget?
facts: Tracking your spending for a month shows where the money goes.

test.q: A company charged me incorrectly. How do I dispute it?
facts: Keeping records of every communication supports your case.

test.q: How do I ask for a raise?
facts: Gathering evidence of your results strengthens the request.

test.q: How do I stay hydrated on a hot day?
facts: Drinking water regularly, before you feel thirsty, keeps you hydrated.

test.q: How should I approach writing an essay?
facts: Starting with an outline keeps the argument organized.

test.q: How can I improve my credit score?
facts: Paying bills on time is the most important factor.

test.q: How do I give feedback to a colleague?
facts: Being specific about the behaviour, not the person, makes feedback easier to act on.

test.q: I'm nervous about giving a presentation. Any advice?
facts: Rehearsing out loud several times builds confidence.
